# How the score is calculated

Every benchmark is a different ruler. A model can score 90% on an easy quiz and 30% on research-level maths, so averaging percentages says little. Instead we line every test up on one shared scale and read off where each model sits. This is **item response theory**, the method exam boards use to put different exam papers on the same scale:

```text
result[model, run] ≈ a[test] · score[model] + d[run]
```

- **a** is a test's sharpness: how many points of result one step of ability is worth. Every run of the same test shares it, learned from all of them together. Saturated tests get a small a and count for less.
- **d** is the level of one evaluator's run of a test. Runs of the same test scatter around a common level by an amount fitted from the data (about 4 points for text models), so an evaluator whose setup runs hot or cold can't move anyone's score, while a small run, such as a lab comparing its new model only with its previous one, is also read against everyone else's runs of that test. A result is read against the other models in its run, so a run needs at least two models and a test at least three across its runs. Sparser results stay visible as raw evidence. Lab-reported results are labelled.
- Percentages are fit as proportions after removing the guessing rate (25% on four-option multiple choice), on a log-odds scale. A result near 0% or 100% says little about how far beyond that edge a model is, so it counts for less. Error ratios use −log(error + 0.005), preserving errors above 100% caused by insertions. Ratings use a linear transformation. Stored raw values are unchanged.
- A failed run, such as one flagged by its source or one far below random guessing because the answers couldn't be parsed, stays visible on the model page but doesn't count.
- Models with few results are pulled toward the middle and get a wider **±**; \* marks scores from fewer than three results, and † scores where every result so far was reported by the model's own maker. Makers' numbers are used like anyone else's, read against the other runs of the same test; the mark only says no one else has checked them yet.
- Task filters recalculate scores using only that task’s reviewed evaluations. Models need task evidence to appear. Compare within the same task and connected set, not against overall scores. Agent measurements depend on the evaluated harness, tools and reasoning effort.
- Arena Agent’s signed IPS effects retain their raw units and are divided by a fixed 0.1 for the latent fit. They are not Elo or success rates. The aggregate is counted once, without duplicate component signals.
- All model sets are listed together by default. Overall scores use the largest connected set; models without a shared scale are not yet calibrated. Under Extra, filter to a set without changing scores, or choose scores within that set. Each scale has mean 50, sd 15; scores from different scales are not comparable. Scores shift as new models arrive.
- ± is uncertainty within this statistical model, not a guarantee of real-world performance or a validated confidence interval.

## Where each score comes from

A score is a weighted average of what each result says on its own. A result's weight is **a² ÷ σ²**: how sharply its test separates models, divided by how noisy the test is. The rest is the prior, a pull toward the middle that matters only for models with few results. Each line splits one text model's score by test:

- [GPT-6 Astra](model/gpt-6-astra.md) (highest score, 88 ±1 from 39 results): EBR-bench (Epoch) 10% · Arena Agent (October 2026 aggregate IPS) 7.1% · Arena WebDev (Code Arena) 6.4% · Mystery Game Puzzles (Epoch) 6.0% · Furniture Assembly (Epoch) 5.6% · other tests 65% · prior 0.2%
- [Hy4 preview (770B-A49B)](model/hy4-preview.md) (best open weights, 79 ±1 from 15 results): Arena Agent (October 2026 aggregate IPS) 22% · Arena WebDev (Code Arena) 20% · SWE-bench Pro (split unspecified) 7.1% · GPQA Diamond 7.1% · Terminal-Bench 2.1 5.7% · other tests 37% · prior 0.6%
- [EXAONE 3.5 7.8B Instruct](model/exaone-3-5-7-8b.md) (middle of the table, 50 ±4\* from 2 results): Arena-Hard (version/judge unspecified) 58% · IFEval (aggregation unspecified) 36% · prior 6.0%
- [GPT-4 Turbo Preview (1106)](model/gpt-4-1106-preview.md) (best from 2023, 54 ±1 from 20 results): HumanEval 15% · HumanEval+ 14% · AlpacaEval 2 length-controlled 13% · LiveBench 2024-07-26 13% · MATH level 5 7.7% · other tests 38% · prior 0.1%
- [GPT-5.2 Chat (2026-02-10)](model/gpt-5-2-chat-latest-20260210.md) (fewest results near the top (*), 75 ±3\* from 2 results): LMArena (text) 56% · Arena vision (style controlled) 41% · prior 2.9%
- [Step 5 Preview](model/step-5-preview.md) (best comparison-only model, 75 ±1 from 4 results): Arena Agent (October 2026 aggregate IPS) 36% · Arena WebDev (Code Arena) 32% · LMArena (text) 18% · Arena vision (style controlled) 13% · prior 1.0%

**Can one hard test dominate?** For the models at the very top, partly. FrontierMath supplies 20% of the evidence behind the top 20 text models' scores, because it is one of the few tests that still separates them, and with little noise. Across all 1116 text models it supplies 2.1%. Overlapping tests count separately: thirteen monthly MathArena sets are thirteen results. We tested a model that learns which tests overlap and discounts them; it ranked models worse on tests it hadn't seen, so we don't use it.

## Prior art

- Epoch AI's Capabilities Index fits the same kind of model to AI benchmarks: each benchmark has a difficulty and a slope, and each model one capability ([“A Rosetta Stone for AI Benchmarks”](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.00193)). We differ in giving each evaluator's run its own level, pooled toward the test's other runs, and in reading every result against the other models in its run.
- LMArena ranks models from head-to-head human votes with a Bradley–Terry model ([Chatbot Arena paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.04132)). We use its ratings as tests among many.
- HELM reports head-to-head win rates: the share of comparisons, across all scenarios, where a model beats another ([HELM paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.09110)).
- How we chose (7 October 2026): we hid whole tests and checked whether each method put models in the same order as the hidden test. This method got about 85% of text-model pairs right; an average win rate got about 77%, and a Bayesian model with extra hidden skills about 82%. On 8 October we pooled run levels: scoring 181 text models from their makers' own numbers alone, pooled levels landed closer to their full-data scores (typical error 2.3 points against 2.7), at a small cost in predicting results within the same run.

## Running models locally

RAM is a rough estimate from parameter count, precision and runtime headroom, not a measured peak. Actual use depends on the engine, batch size, context and KV cache. A listed context window is the provider ceiling; the RAM estimate does not promise that the full window fits on your machine.

Scores describe the published model evaluation. A quantized download may perform differently; we currently apply no numeric quantization penalty. Unknown prices and speeds are left blank or marked unknown. Unknown prices never pass a finite budget filter. API prices use base token rates blended three input tokens to one output token; check the provider for tiers and surcharges.

Model pages include sourced reference speed measurements with their hardware, engine, precision and workload. They are not automatically assigned to another download or machine. The main speed column stays blank when no matching measurement is verified; bandwidth predictions remain disabled.

API speeds are our own measurements: we stream a fixed prompt to each model three times, pinned to the provider whose price we list, and publish the raw runs in [api-speed.json](../data/api-speed.json). You can add local speeds for your own machine with the [bench script](../bench.sh); submissions are checked and reviewed before they appear.

## Benchmarks

18566 results, each with a source link. Download the [raw results](../data/results.json), [benchmark definitions](../data/benchmarks.json), or [rankings as JSON](https://whatmodel.sh/api?format=json&all=1).

**Share of evidence** is how much of all the weight behind a category's scores comes from that run, averaged over its scored models.

## Sources

Benchmark results and API prices use the licensed datasets listed below, plus scores and prices that model makers publish for their own models, recorded by hand as facts and labelled lab-reported. Missing coverage is withheld. Sources do not endorse this site. Scores and rankings are our calculations, not the sources' own figures.

Our contributions to the numerical data compilation, adaptations and derived scores are [CC BY-SA 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/). Source-specific licences and notices remain in force. Changes include model-name mapping, unit conversion, selection of settings and the calculation of relative scores. The [source register](../data/sources.json) includes attribution and licence notices. Share-alike extracts in [data/extracts](../data/extracts) retain those terms.
